title: Bartleby, the Scrivener
focus: refusal as a mystery the narrator cannot solve

teacherSummary.text: An elderly Wall Street lawyer hires a pale copyist, Bartleby, who works well until he begins answering every request with 'I would prefer not to.' He stops copying, lives in the office, and will not leave. Unable to dismiss him, the lawyer moves his offices; Bartleby is taken to the Tombs prison, where he refuses to eat and dies. The lawyer learns Bartleby once worked in the Dead Letter Office: 'Ah Bartleby! Ah humanity!'

segments.activity: Model the close reading of the anchor quotation using the written think-aloud below.
segments.script: First, meaning. I read “I would prefer not to” slowly and put it in my own words: Asked to do his work, Bartleby says he would prefer not to. Next, craft. I notice the phrase is mild and conditional, not "I will not," which makes it impossible to argue with. The strongest word is “prefer”: it is a word of polite choice, and it turns refusal into something gentle and maddening. Then, effect. What is the effect of Bartleby's polite refusal? My answer: The effect of Bartleby's polite refusal is to paralyze the lawyer, who cannot handle a refusal that is calm and unexplained; the line exposes how much his office depends on everyone obeying.

hsJunior.note: Emphasize structure and ambiguity; students should name where the text leaves matters open.

hsSenior.note: Weigh competing interpretations; students should defend the stronger reading.

ap.note: Treat each evaluative item as a thesis rehearsal: defensible claim, purposeful evidence, commentary on choices.

collegeFreshman.note: Add the extension: connect answers to historical context and one secondary perspective.

collegeSophomore.note: Use the extensions: genre and period conventions, and a published critic.

collegeJunior.note: Use the extensions: name a critical method and test it against the passage.

collegeSenior.note: Use the extensions: connect the story to the whole work and the scholarship.

graduate.note: Use the extensions: position answers in a critical conversation and the textual history.
